questions.stem: Which of the following articles is a product of basketry?
questions.explanation: Hats, mats, baskets and fans woven from raffia or cane are basketry products.

questions.stem: Making a chair seat by weaving cane strands across a wooden frame belongs to the area of basketry called
questions.explanation: Frame work involves weaving or lashing materials onto a rigid frame.

questions.stem: One economic benefit of learning basketry is that it
options: requires costly imported machines to start a business
questions.explanation: Basketry skills can be used to earn a living.

questions.topic: History, Social, Cultural and Economic Importance
questions.stem: Long before plastics, farmers in many Nigerian communities used woven baskets mainly to
options: fetch and store water from deep wells
questions.explanation: Baskets carried and stored crops such as yams, grains and kola.

questions.topic: History, Social, Cultural and Economic Importance
questions.stem: Woven raffia costumes and masks used in masquerades show the
options: agricultural use of chemical fertiliser on farms
questions.explanation: Masquerade costumes and ritual objects show basketry's cultural role.

questions.stem: Raffia products from Ikot Ekpene are well known mainly because the town is
options: a seaport for importing cane from abroad
a centre of raffia craft production
questions.explanation: Ikot Ekpene is a famous raffia craft centre in Akwa Ibom State.

questions.stem: A basket maker who accepts only the number of orders that can be finished on time is showing good
questions.explanation: Planning work within available time is time management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a synthetic basketry material?
questions.explanation: Plastic strips are man-made; the others are natural.

questions.stem: Water hyacinth, a weed that blocks waterways, can be dried and used as
questions.explanation: Dried hyacinth stems are woven into baskets and mats.

questions.stem: Stiff materials such as thick cane or bamboo strips are most suitable for
questions.explanation: Rigid materials form frameworks; pliable ones are used as weavers.

questions.stem: Split palm leaves are dried in the shade rather than in strong sun in order to
options: prevent them becoming brittle and discoloured
make them grow longer and become much thicker
questions.explanation: Shade drying keeps materials pliable and evenly coloured.

questions.stem: Treating stored raffia with a suitable insecticide or keeping it dry mainly prevents
questions.explanation: Pests and moulds damage stored natural materials.

questions.stem: Splitting cane lengthwise into strips of uniform width is called
questions.explanation: A cleave splits cane into even strips.

questions.stem: Round-nose pliers are used in basketry mainly for
questions.explanation: Pliers grip, bend and shape stakes and borders.

questions.stem: A screw block in basketry is used to
options: polish and varnish the finished work neatly
hold the stakes of a square base in position
questions.explanation: The screw block clamps stakes while a square or rectangular base is woven.

questions.stem: Tools should be cleaned, dried and oiled after use mainly to
options: prevent rusting and prolong their life
questions.explanation: Proper care prevents rust and damage.

questions.stem: The element of design produced by the surface feel of the woven material is
questions.explanation: Texture is how a surface feels or appears to feel.

questions.stem: Using thin and thick weavers next to one another in a basket introduces variety mainly in
questions.explanation: Different weaver thicknesses create lines of varying weight.

questions.stem: A round tray with a pattern radiating from the centre to the edge shows
questions.explanation: Radial balance spreads from a centre point.

questions.stem: Placing one bright red band in an otherwise natural-coloured basket mainly creates
questions.explanation: A single contrasting feature becomes a focal point.

questions.stem: Creating a basket design from pictures formed in the mind without looking at any object is designing from
questions.explanation: Imaginative design comes from the mind; observation uses objects in view.

questions.stem: In basketry, the cross formed by laying stakes over each other to begin a round base is the
questions.explanation: The slath is the crossed group of base stakes that the weaving opens out.

questions.stem: Bending the base stakes upwards to begin the side of a basket is called
questions.explanation: Upsetting turns the stakes up to start the sides.

questions.stem: Working two or more weavers together as one in a randing pattern is
questions.explanation: Slewing uses several weavers side by side.

questions.stem: Twisting two weavers round each other between widely spaced stakes to create an openwork pattern is
questions.explanation: Fitching gives openwork with spaces between rows.

questions.stem: In pairing, two weavers are used so that
options: each passes alternately in front of and behind stakes, crossing between them
one weaver lies behind all stakes
the weavers are knotted firmly together at every single stake on the round
questions.explanation: Pairing twists two weavers round each other between stakes.

questions.topic: Designing Articles to Suit Specific Needs
questions.stem: A basket intended to hold heavy yams should be designed mainly for
questions.explanation: Function determines design; heavy loads need strong construction.

questions.topic: Designing Articles to Suit Specific Needs
questions.stem: When designing a bread basket for a restaurant, the most important requirement is that it is
options: covered with sharp edges and splinters
questions.explanation: Food baskets must be hygienic and safe.

questions.stem: Planting more cane and raffia palms after harvesting helps to
options: increase bush burning in the dry season
questions.explanation: Replanting sustains supply.

questions.stem: Basket makers can compete better with cheap plastic containers by
questions.explanation: Quality, innovation and good marketing help crafts compete.

questions.stem: Tying the loose ends of weavers neatly at the end of work is part of
questions.explanation: Finishing includes trimming, tying, binding and wrapping.

questions.stem: Weaving with naturally coloured and dyed weavers to form stripes is a method of
questions.explanation: Coloured weavers create decorative patterns.

questions.stem: Lightly rubbing a finished bamboo article with fine abrasive paper before varnishing is
questions.explanation: Sanding smooths the surface for finishing.

questions.stem: A collection of photographs and samples of a basket maker's best works is a
questions.explanation: A portfolio showcases the maker's skill.

questions.stem: The part of a business plan that describes who will buy the products and how they will be reached is the
questions.explanation: The marketing plan covers customers, pricing and promotion.

questions.stem: Displaying baskets at a trade fair mainly helps the craftsman to
questions.explanation: Fairs and exhibitions promote products and attract buyers.

questions.stem: Placing several individually wrapped baskets in a large carton for transport is
questions.explanation: Outer cartons that group products are secondary or transit packaging.

questions.stem: Twelve fruit baskets require materials worth N450 each and N3,000 for other costs. The total production cost is
A workshop has fixed costs of N24,000 per month and a variable cost of N800 per basket. If each basket sells for N2,400, the number of baskets that must be sold to break even is
questions.explanation: Break-even = 24,000 / (2,400 - 800) = 15 baskets.

questions.stem: The cost of materials which increases as more baskets are produced is a
questions.explanation: Variable costs change with output; rent is fixed.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between pliable and rigid basketry materials, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) State three qualities of a good basketry material. [3 marks]
(c) Explain three ways of preserving the sources of basketry materials. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Pliable materials bend easily without breaking, e.g. raffia, grasses, palm leaves, thin cane (any two)
3 marks: Rigid materials are stiff and keep their shape, e.g. bamboo, thick cane, wire (any two)
1 mark: Strong and durable
1 mark: Flexible enough when prepared
1 mark: Readily available, of uniform size and free of defects
2 marks: Replanting/re-afforestation of cane, raffia and bamboo
2 marks: Avoiding bush burning and indiscriminate cutting
2 marks: Harvesting mature stems only and leaving young shoots to grow
questions.explanation: Pliable materials such as raffia bend; rigid ones like bamboo hold shape. Good materials are strong, workable and readily available. Sources are preserved by replanting, avoiding bush burning and selective harvesting.

questions.stem:
(a) Classify basketry tools into cutting, measuring and shaping tools, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) State three safety precautions to observe when using basketry tools. [6 marks]
(c) Describe how any one basketry tool can be improvised locally. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Cutting tools, e.g. knife, side cutters, shears, cleave
2 marks: Measuring tools, e.g. tape measure, rule, calipers
2 marks: Shaping/working tools, e.g. bodkin, round-nose pliers, rapping iron
2 marks: Keep sharp tools covered and cut away from the body
2 marks: Use the right tool for each job and keep the work area tidy
2 marks: Store tools safely after use, out of children's reach
3 marks: Correct improvisation, e.g. a bodkin from a sharpened hardwood or a large nail fitted with a wooden handle
questions.explanation: Cutting tools include knives and side cutters; measuring tools include tape and rule; shaping tools include bodkin and pliers. Cover blades, cut away from the body and store tools well. A bodkin can be improvised from hardwood or a nail with a handle.

questions.stem: Describe the steps in preparing raffia for weaving a coloured mat. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Harvest young raffia leaves at the right stage
2 marks: Strip the fibre from the leaf surface
2 marks: Dry in shade to keep fibres pliable and pale
2 marks: Sort and grade by length and width
2 marks: Scour/wash to remove dirt before dyeing
3 marks: Dye in prepared dye bath, using a fixing agent, then rinse
2 marks: Dry the dyed fibres and store in a dry, pest-free place
questions.explanation: Harvest young leaves, strip fibre, shade-dry, grade, wash, dye with a fixing agent and rinse, then dry and store safely.

questions.stem: Describe the following basketry techniques, stating one article for which each is suitable: (a) coiling (b) plaiting (c) waling. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Coiling: a bundle of core material is spiralled round and stitched or bound to the previous row
2 marks: Coiling article, e.g. trays, bowls or Hausa food covers (faifai)
3 marks: Plaiting: flat strands interlaced over and under one another, often diagonally or at right angles
2 marks: Plaiting article, e.g. mats, hats, fans
3 marks: Waling: three or more weavers worked in turn in front of and behind stakes to make a strong rope-like band
2 marks: Waling use, e.g. strengthening the base or rim of a laundry or shopping basket
questions.explanation: Coiling builds a spiral bound row on row (trays, bowls). Plaiting interlaces flat strands (mats, hats). Waling uses three or more weavers to make strong bands at bases and rims.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the difference between decoration and finishing in basketry. [4 marks]
(b) Describe four methods of decorating a basket. [8 marks]
(c) State three finishing processes. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Decoration adds beauty and interest to an article
2 marks: Finishing makes the article neat, durable and ready for use
2 marks: Using coloured or dyed weavers to create patterns
2 marks: Weave variations such as fitching, waling or slewing to create texture
2 marks: Scorching/pokerwork to darken parts of the material
2 marks: Attaching beads, cowries, shells or leather as complementary objects
1 mark: Trimming loose ends
1 mark: Binding or wrapping rims and handles
1 mark: Singeing, sanding or varnishing
questions.explanation: Decoration beautifies; finishing makes the article neat and durable. Decoration uses coloured weavers, weave variations, scorching and attachments; finishing includes trimming, binding and varnishing or singeing.

questions.stem:
(a) State five items that should be included in a business plan for a basketry enterprise. [5 marks]
(b) Explain five ways of promoting basketry products. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Business description and objectives
1 mark: Products and services
1 mark: Market analysis and marketing strategy
1 mark: Operations: materials, tools, workshop, staff
1 mark: Financial plan: capital, costs, pricing and projected profit
2 marks: Exhibitions and trade fairs
2 marks: Social media and online sales platforms
2 marks: Attractive packaging and branding
2 marks: Supplying hotels, tourist centres and gift shops
2 marks: Advertisement, flyers, word of mouth and discounts
questions.explanation: A business plan covers description, products, market, operations and finances. Products are promoted through fairs, online platforms, branding, tourist outlets and advertisement.
